summary: A formal statement of the requirements that gateways between networks using the Internet protocols must meet. It served as the official specification for such gateways, replacing RFC 985. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1812.

eli5.summary: It is the official checklist for the machines that connect networks together, saying what they have to do to be allowed on the Internet.

questions: what are the requirements for internet gateways
what is the difference between a gateway and a router
what were the original gateway requirements
subtitle: The 1987 checklist of what an IP router, then called a gateway, had to do to belong on the Internet.

tldr.problem: Vendors were building gateways to connect networks that use the Internet protocols, but the specifications were scattered across many documents and in places ambiguous or incomplete.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gathers the protocols a gateway must implement, how it attaches to common networks, the algorithms it needs for routing, buffering and filtering, and the operation and maintenance facilities it must offer, adding guidance where the underlying specifications were unclear.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1009 is Historic. It obsoleted RFC 985 and was itself replaced by RFC 1812.

facts.label: Minimum reassembly buffer
facts.value: At least the larger of the interface MTUs and 576

sections.title: What a Gateway Is and Why Requirements Were Needed
sections.content:
RFC 1009 is a formal statement of the requirements for gateways used between networks that support the Internet protocols. It was written to support National Science Foundation research programs, but the requirements are stated generally. The goal is guidance for vendors whose products might be used in an Internet application.

The document is careful with terms. A packet is the unit on a physical network, a datagram is the unit of the IP protocol, and a gateway is an IP-level router. A gateway connects to two or more networks, has a physical interface and an IP address on each, and chooses the next hop for every datagram using a routing data-base. Gateways are grouped into autonomous systems under a single operations organization, which use an interior gateway protocol (IGP) inside and the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) between systems.

The RFC also warns against casual "embedded gateways" in host operating systems. A host with only one network interface should not act as a gateway, and one that does must meet all the gateway requirements.
sections.eli5: A gateway is like a road junction between towns: it looks at where each parcel is going and sends it down the right road. This paper lists what a good junction must do.

sections.title: Protocols a Gateway Must Support
sections.content:
Every gateway implements IP and ICMP. For IP, it must fragment datagrams to fit the next network's MTU, but it does not reassemble datagrams it merely forwards. It must reassemble datagrams addressed to itself, with a reassembly buffer at least as large as the biggest interface MTU and 576. Loose and Strict Source Route are important, and Record Route and Timestamp must be supported. Class D and Class E destinations must be ignored by a gateway not taking part in those experiments.

The RFC lists special address forms, such as limited broadcast and the loopback range, and says which may appear only as sources or destinations. For ICMP, it discusses Destination Unreachable, Redirect, Source Quench, Time Exceeded, Parameter Problem, Address Mask, Timestamp, Echo and the Information request. It recommends that gateways send only host Redirects, and requires code for Source Quench with a configurable rate limit. Echo must be implemented.

Beyond IP, the RFC points to EGP for exchanging reachability between autonomous systems, ARP (including proxy ARP) for LANs, and several interior protocols: GGP, SPF-based protocols and RIP, plus the Hello protocol. RIP uses a hop count with 16 as "infinity" and needs measures such as a hold-down (typically 60 seconds) to avoid counting to infinity. Multicast with IGMP is called experimental, and datagrams with Class D addresses must be dropped silently.
sections.eli5: All the gateways have to speak the same few languages so they can pass parcels along and tell each other when something goes wrong. They also have to stay calm and ignore addresses meant for experiments.

sections.title: Attaching to Different Networks
sections.content:
A gateway must be able to send and receive IP datagrams up to the MTU of each network it connects to. The RFC describes the common attachment types: public data networks over X.25 (normal MTU 576, negotiable upward), ARPANET through 1822 interfaces (MTU 1007), ARPANET through DDN Standard X.25 (effective MTU 1007 for compatibility), and Ethernet or IEEE 802 networks (MTU 1500).

On IEEE 802 networks IP uses an LSAP header plus a SNAP header, 8 octets in total. For serial lines there was no single Internet standard link protocol, so the RFC suggests options such as X.25 LAPB, HDLC framing, the Xerox synchronous point-to-point protocol or a serial line framing protocol. It also suggests compressing traffic on serial lines and numbering such lines with subnets, so that they do not eat up routing data-base space.
sections.eli5: Different roads have different weight limits for trucks. A gateway has to know each road's limit so its parcels fit.

sections.title: Routing, Resource Sharing and Safety Rules
sections.content:
The RFC places no restriction on the routing algorithm or metric, but lists features a good one must have. It must notice link or gateway failures and switch paths, with a design objective of less than the typical TCP user time-out (one minute is a safe assumption). It must suppress routing loops, keep its control traffic from disrupting normal operation, and keep the routing data-base from growing out of control. Default routes must be used with care.

Subnets add their own rules: a subnetted gateway must consider the address mask, routing updates outside a subnet cluster contain nets and never subnets, and a different mask must be configurable for each interface. Resource allocation should be fair: a fast interface must not starve slow ones of buffers. Nagle's fair queueing idea is mentioned, to be added later if research supports it.

Gateways should filter forbidden destination addresses and avoid putting them in routing updates. They must not forward a datagram that arrives by local-network broadcast, and must not send an ICMP error for it, to prevent packet avalanches. The TTL is an 8-bit field in seconds, each gateway decrements it by at least one, and a datagram whose TTL reaches zero must be discarded.
sections.eli5: A good gateway shares its limited space fairly, finds a new road quickly when one is closed, and never passes along suspicious parcels that could cause a traffic jam.

sections.title: Operation and Maintenance
sections.content:
Gateways normally run unattended, so the RFC treats operation and maintenance as essential. Operators work from a network operation center (NOC), so a gateway must support remote control and monitoring through an Internet path. The direct approach, where the gateway speaks standard protocols such as UDP or TCP, is preferred. No Internet standard existed yet for control and monitoring protocols.

Required functions include hardware diagnosis that works with on-site tools, dump and reboot on command from the NOC, a watchdog timer for stand-alone gateways, configuration without rebooting, status and statistics retrieval in answer to polling, and rate-limited exception reports ("traps"). The RFC lists representative configuration parameters, such as the subnet mask, MTU, EGP neighbors, static routes, proxy ARP, Source Quench settings and address filters, many of them settable per interface.
sections.eli5: Since nobody sits next to a gateway all day, the people in charge must be able to check on it and fix it from far away.

sections.title: NSFNET-Specific Requirements
sections.content:
Appendix B covers issues of special concern to the NSF networking community. Vendors are urged to treat extensibility and periodic upgrades as fundamental. NSF gateways must at a minimum support Ethernet and serial line connections, and Ethernet is named the common point of demarcation between different vendors' systems.

The text admits there was no "open IGP" yet. Approaches then in use were a proprietary IGP with EGP to the outside, RIP despite its lack of a document, and a "gateway daemon" that can speak RIP, Hello and EGP. It also expects a gradual transition to ISO protocols, and encourages designs able to carry both IP and ISO CLNS. Access control and accounting were not yet required.
sections.eli5: The last part is the extra rules for one big research network, including tips about getting ready for changes down the road.
